newsitem.title: UK: Mark crosses steady as dlr/Europe buying dominates.
newsitem.headline: Mark crosses steady as dlr/Europe buying dominates.

text.p: The mark was treading water against its European crosses, even as it sank to its lowest level in seven and a half years against the dollar, which continued to storm higher against major currencies.
Traders said there was not much interest in the European crosses this morning as the currency market was riveted to the dollar's moves.

Prospects of a broad-based European monetary union with a watered-down single currency still held sway, prompting buying of dollars against the mark, French franc and other European currencies expected to be involved in EMU, they said.

"The move is still one of safe-haven dollar buying across Europe (currencies) on EMU concerns and so on, although this is making the mark's tone slightly softer against the Europeans," said one trader at a Japanese bank in London.
The mark was at 3.3708/13 French francs at against its late Friday European level of 3.709/14, while against the lira it was at 973.60/70 against 973.79/99.
Traders said they did not expect the mark to weaken much today, citing buying interest for mark/Paris at the round-figure 3.70 francs level and for mark/lira around 969-970.
Analysts said the stagnation on the mark crosses was only to be expected.

"It's a move in anticipation of European monetary union, so there's no real reason why the mark should be moving on the crosses. What's happening is that the whole European currency bloc is weakening together against the dollar," said Julian Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko Europe.
Among the European currencies, traders said the Swiss franc and some of the Scandinavian currencies were benefitting from their safe-haven status outside the EMU group.
"Like the Scandis, the Swiss franc has been bought up on the EMU concerns, and though it's pulling back a bit now, it's well supported on the downside," the bank trader said.
The Swiss franc was at 82.32/34 centimes per mark, up from its late Friday level of 82.44/46. It had risen to an 11-month high of 80.85 centimes against the mark on Thursday.
Against the Swedish crown, the mark was edging off its earlier lows and was at 4.2890.20 at 0905 GMT against Friday's close at 4.2860/90.
But there was some doubt as to how much further European currencies not involved in the EMU project could rise on worries about a broad-based single currency.
For one thing, analysts said, the Scandinavian currencies did not have enough liquidity and were too volatile to become a reliable safe-haven currency.
"The Swiss franc has gained on the EMU story, but it's not as good a safe haven as sterling," said Nikko's Jessop.

"There's been no growth in the Swiss economy so the Swiss central bank will definitely try to keep the currency down, whereas in the UK they would rather keep tight monetary policy. So although the Bank (of England) is not keen about a strengthening currency, it can't do anything about it," he said.
